name: Inflation surge
brief: After a period of heavy stimulus, spending is booming while supply chains are jammed. Inflation is more than three times the target and unemployment is at a record low. The policy rate is still near zero, and the central bank balance sheet is still swollen from earlier rounds of QE.
challenge: Bring inflation back to 2% without pushing the economy into a deep recession.

events.title: Global energy prices cool
events.text: Oil prices fall 15% from last quarter, easing pressure on production costs.

events.title: Unions win 7% pay rises
events.text: Many industries raise wages to catch up with past inflation. Risk of a wage–price spiral.

events.title: Housing market stalls
events.text: Home sales drop sharply as mortgage rates bite.

name: Demand-driven recession
brief: Business confidence has collapsed after a trade shock. Orders are falling, factories are cutting shifts and unemployment is rising fast. Inflation is still close to target but drifting down.
challenge: Stop the slide and bring unemployment back to its natural rate without creating inflation later.

events.title: Exports keep falling
events.text: Exports are down 8% year on year; industrial parks are laying off workers.

events.title: Firms shelve expansion plans
events.text: A survey shows 40% of businesses are postponing new investment.

events.title: New trade deal signed
events.text: Export markets reopen and business confidence improves.

name: Financial crisis
brief: Several large banks have suffered heavy losses and credit markets have almost frozen: lending spreads have soared and firms cannot borrow. The policy rate is only 1%, close to zero.
challenge: With little room left to cut rates, use QE and forward guidance to ease financial conditions.

events.title: Another bank fails
events.text: Depositors panic and banks stop lending to each other.

events.title: Government guarantees deposits
events.text: Fiscal policy (outside your control) helps calm depositors.

events.title: Firms start hiring again
events.text: New business registrations rise for the first time in two years.

name: Stagflation (oil shock)
brief: World oil prices have doubled. Rising production costs are pushing prices up while output falls. People are starting to believe inflation will stay high for a long time.
challenge: Face the hardest trade-off: tighten to anchor inflation expectations, or ease to protect jobs?

events.title: Conflict disrupts oil supply
events.text: Oil jumps another 30%. Fuel, transport and food prices all rise.

events.title: Household inflation expectations rise
events.text: Survey: people expect prices to rise 6% over the next year.

events.title: Oil prices start to fall
events.text: Producers raise output and oil drops 20%.

name: Soft landing
brief: The economy is growing well, inflation is a little above target and the labour market is tight. Everything looks fine, but risk is building up in property lending.
challenge: Guide inflation gently back to 2% and react in time when a shock hits.

events.title: Regional bank turmoil
events.text: Three property lenders run into liquidity trouble. Lending spreads jump.

events.title: Consumers tighten their belts
events.text: Retail sales fall for a second month in a row.

children.text: The interest rate the central bank charges when it lends to commercial banks for short periods. In the US it is the federal funds rate; in Vietnam, the State Bank's refinancing rate is one of its policy rates.

Policy rate up → banks raise lending rates → firms invest less and households borrow less for homes and cars → aggregate demand falls → firms hire fewer people and find it harder to raise prices → inflation falls.
Borrowing costs change almost immediately; spending and investment respond after 1–3 quarters; inflation is slowest.
It cannot go much below 0%. It does not fix the cause of a supply shock (such as an oil price spike).

In 2022 the US Federal Reserve raised its rate from 0–0.25% to 4.25–4.5% to fight the highest inflation in 40 years. In 2023 the State Bank of Vietnam cut its policy rates four times to support growth.

The central bank creates money to buy long-term bonds in the market. Bond prices rise and long-term yields fall, pulling down mortgage and business borrowing rates, even when the policy rate is already at 0%.
The reverse: the central bank sells bonds or lets them mature without reinvesting. Long-term yields rise and financial conditions tighten.
When financial markets are stressed and the policy rate has hit bottom. In this simulation, QE is more powerful when market stress is high.
A very large balance sheet is hard to shrink later and can inflate asset prices. The simulation deducts points when the balance sheet exceeds 35% of GDP.
After the 2008 crisis the Fed bought assets, growing its balance sheet from about $900 billion to about $4.5 trillion. From mid-2022 the Fed began QT.
AD
(aggregate demand, slopes down): total spending by households, firms, government and the rest of the world.
SRAS
(short-run aggregate supply, slopes up): firms produce more when prices are higher.
LRAS
(vertical): potential output Y*, set by labour, capital and technology.
Where AD meets SRAS. Right of LRAS: the economy is overheating. Left of LRAS: spare capacity and high unemployment.
The policy rate, QE/QT and forward guidance shift
AD
: tightening pushes AD left, easing pushes it right, but it takes 1–3 quarters.

entries.term: What the central bank can't do

children.text: It cannot shift SRAS back when oil prices rise, and it cannot move LRAS. When SRAS shifts up (stagflation), every choice about AD means trading off inflation against output.
If people expect high inflation, workers demand higher wages and firms raise prices, so SRAS shifts up. Central bank credibility helps keep SRAS stable.
The vertical axis uses the inflation rate instead of the price level, to match the dashboard. The slopes of the curves are illustrative only.
The central bank announces in advance what it intends to do with interest rates. Because long-term borrowing costs depend on expected future rates, words alone can change financial conditions today.
“We will keep rates low for a long time” → markets expect lower future rates → long-term yields fall → borrowing gets cheaper.
Credibility. Promises from a credible central bank have more effect. Saying one thing and doing another destroys credibility and weakens every tool afterwards.

In August 2011 the Fed said it expected to keep rates exceptionally low “at least through mid-2013”. In 2012 ECB President Mario Draghi pledged to do “whatever it takes” to preserve the euro, and bond yields in several countries fell sharply.
